name: PT M Cash Integrasi Tbk

frontmatter.title: M Cash Integrasi: a diluted claim on a margin recovery
frontmatter.summary: We initiate at HOLD. The DCF pays for the margin recovery management is delivering and comes out above the price, but the parent owns only part of the subsidiaries that earn it, the book floor is depressed, and the convertible notes make the outcome per share uncertain. The parts we can source do not support a stronger call either way.
thesis: The revenue collapse is a mix shift, not a demand collapse: the aggregator that is shrinking carried almost no gross profit, and the blend improves as advertising and SaaS take over.
The parent claim is diluted twice: NFC is majority-owned, DMM reaches the group only through NFC, and the LK allocates most of the consolidated loss to non-controlling interests.
The DCF at our forecast margin path is worth more than the price, the book floor is worth less, and the DCF-weighted blend lands within a few percent of the market.
The convertible notes are the binding constraint rather than the operating business: they exceed parent cash and their extension was unresolved at the reporting date.
The investment portfolio is real but modest at the parent level once each stake is counted at the ownership of the entity that holds it.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results: aggregator run-rate, cloud-advertising fill and any going-concern or emphasis-of-matter language
Convertible note extension or conversion decision for the notes still awaiting an extension
AGMS: dividend decision, auditor reappointment and any further treasury-share or subsidiary transactions

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT M Cash Integrasi Tbk (MCAS) at HOLD with a twelve-month target of Rp213 against Rp199, a total return of 6.9%. The target is the probability-weighted scenario value less the liquidity discount applied to a name this illiquid. The DCF, which pays for the margin recovery the company is actually delivering, is worth Rp224; the price-to-book floor is Rp92; the blend is Rp178 before the twelve-month roll-forward. The debt base behind that is the LK's own: interest-bearing liabilities of IDR422.4bn at 30 September 2026 less cash of IDR143.5bn and restricted time deposits of IDR5.0bn [S3].

The variant view is about mix, not size. The market no longer treats MCAS as a platform, and it is right not to: revenue is shrinking and the aggregator earns almost nothing on it. What may be mispriced is the composition — gross profit has held up while revenue collapsed, cloud advertising earns a real margin, and the cost base is being cut against the smaller top line [S2][S3]. Two things stop that from being a buy. First, the parent owns 51.6% of NFC Indonesia and reaches DMM, the advertising profit engine, only through NFC's 29.3% stake, so the group's effective interest in the segment that earns the margin is a fraction of the consolidated number, and the nine-month accounts allocate IDR34.4bn of the IDR53.8bn net loss to non-controlling interests [S3]. Second, convertible notes of IDR240.9bn are current against cash of IDR143.5bn, and the extension request filed on 30 September 2026 was unresolved at the reporting date [S3]. Equity here is an option on the notes being extended and the margin continuing to recover.

The bear case is a floor, not a forecast. Under the bear shocks the DCF equity value goes to zero, so what remains is the book check at its 35.0% weight: that is the whole mechanism behind the Rp41 bear, which is below any credible recovery value. We read the true downside as the book value itself rather than the mechanical blend. The bull case, in which cloud advertising and SaaS scale and the notes convert cleanly, is worth Rp559, and the base case Rp225.

Three things move the value. First, whether the aggregator decline decelerates: revenue growth of -42.3% in FY2026E with gross margin rising from 5.4% to 8.0% by FY2030E is the DCF's engine, and the 9M2026 segment note shows advertising and SaaS gross margins improving even as the aggregator shrinks, which is the mix shift in miniature [S3]. Second, the notes: a conversion at a discount is dilutive and a cash repayment is not fundable, so the terms matter per share. Third, the listed stakes and the portfolio: we carry the operating businesses through the consolidated DCF and the investment portfolio at each holder's actual ownership, and explain in the valuation section why a sum-of-the-parts at market marks would flatter the target rather than test it.

M Cash Integrasi began as a cash-based top-up and bill-payment network for warungs and small retailers, then widened into digital product distribution, digital out-of-home advertising, software services and electric mobility. Indonesian digital payments have moved from cash and bank transfers toward QRIS, the national QR standard, which made acceptance cheap for small merchants and commoditised the distribution layer that MCAS originally monetised. The company's controlling shareholder is itself a listed investment vehicle, a structure that is common on the Indonesia Stock Exchange among family-controlled technology groups.

MCAS reports four segments. The digital product aggregator distributes mobile credit, data, vouchers, bill payments and similar products through a network of partner outlets and members; it generated IDR3,644.0bn of revenue and IDR27.6bn of gross profit in FY2025 [S2]. Digital cloud advertising operates a network of digital signage screens and generated IDR279.8bn of revenue and IDR109.5bn of gross profit [S2]. SaaS and IT services generated IDR141.2bn of revenue and IDR25.0bn of gross profit, and the clean energy products and services segment generated IDR148.2bn of revenue and IDR4.4bn of gross profit [S2].

The operating base is real but small relative to the revenue line. At the end of FY2025 the group operated 28,996 digital signage screens, served 268,819 aggregator members, ran 422 battery swap stations and carried 583,423,174 SaaS notifications [S2]. Those assets support the advertising and SaaS segments, which are the parts of the group with defensible margins; the aggregator's member base is the distribution channel through which third-party digital products are sold.

The group structure explains the valuation. MCAS owns 51.6% of PT NFC Indonesia Tbk and 42.2% of PT Telefast Indonesia Tbk, and it consolidates both [S2][S3]. NFC is the listed subsidiary that carries most of the group's revenue and most of the separate non-controlling interest; Telefast is the smaller supply-chain and digital-product affiliate, itself listed. DMM, the cloud-advertising business, sits inside NFC, which holds 29.3% of it [S3], and DMM's 20.0% stake in ZKDigimax, a smart-retail hardware joint venture, is likewise held inside the group rather than by the parent [S2]. The parent therefore controls the operating companies without owning all of their economics, which is why the consolidated accounts show a large minority interest and a comparatively small parent equity balance — and why a consolidated enterprise value has to be apportioned rather than simply divided by the share count.

Strategy as stated by management is to prioritise segments with a clear path to scale and profitability while improving operating efficiency across the group [S2]. In practice the FY2025 annual report describes continued expansion of the advertising screen network and the aggregator member ecosystem, alongside the electric-vehicle infrastructure build-out [S2]. Clean energy is the newest leg: Volta, the group's electric motorcycle brand, has a partnership intended to put a large fleet of electric motorcycles on Indonesian roads [S5], with battery swap stations as the supporting infrastructure [S2]. That segment is close to break-even at the gross-profit line and consumes cash.

On competitive position MCAS is a challenger, not a leader. The aggregator competes with bank-owned payment apps, e-wallet platforms and other distributor networks, all of which can reach the same merchants directly; the advertising network competes with conventional out-of-home and other digital signage operators; the SaaS business competes with specialist software vendors. The group's advantage is its merchant and member network and the physical screen estate, which are difficult to replicate quickly but do not confer pricing power. The annual report's own emphasis on portfolio discipline and cost control is a tacit acknowledgement that growth is no longer the constraint [S2].

Indonesian digital distribution works through a layered network: product principals sell airtime, data and vouchers to aggregators, aggregators sell to distributors and outlets, and outlets serve end customers. Each layer takes a thin spread, so revenue is large relative to gross profit and working capital is dominated by inventory and receivables. Digital out-of-home advertising has better economics because the scarce asset is the screen location and the advertiser pays for attention rather than for a recharge. The two businesses sit in the same group but have almost nothing in common economically.

The addressable market is growing. Bank Indonesia reported 67.2% year-on-year growth in QRIS transaction volume in August 2026, with digital payment transaction volume rising by more than two-fifths year on year [S6]. The same release notes growth in mobile banking and internet banking volumes, and continued expansion of the QRIS merchant base [S6]. On any reading, Indonesian consumers and merchants are transacting digitally at a rapidly rising rate.

MCAS is not capturing that growth. Group revenue fell to IDR4,737.7bn in FY2025 from IDR7,143.6bn in FY2024 and IDR11,697.1bn in FY2023, and the first nine months of FY2026 came in at IDR2,132.2bn [S2][S3]. A distributor whose revenue shrinks while the underlying transaction market grows is losing share, either because merchants are moving to bank and e-wallet rails or because the group is deliberately exiting low-margin volume. The segment disclosure points to the latter as the main driver: the aggregator is the segment that is contracting, and it is the segment with negligible gross margin [S2].

The competitive dynamics are unfavourable for the aggregator layer. QRIS is an interoperable standard, which means a merchant can accept payment through any participating app without going through an MCAS outlet. Banks and e-wallets have direct relationships with merchants and can bundle top-up and bill payment into their own apps at no incremental distribution cost. The aggregator's historical advantage, physical reach into small retailers, is being eroded as smartphone penetration and QR acceptance spread. The group's response, moving toward advertising and software, is rational, but those markets are smaller and are served by specialists [S2][S6].

Five forces, in brief. Supplier power is high: the product principals are telcos and content owners who set wholesale prices and can deal directly with large merchants. Buyer power is high: outlets and members can switch distributor on price, and end customers are indifferent to the brand behind a top-up. The threat of new entrants is high in distribution and moderate in digital signage, where site leases and capital are barriers. Substitutes are strong: bank apps, e-wallets and QRIS itself substitute for the aggregator's core function. Rivalry is intense and price-based, which is why gross margin in the aggregator is a rounding error. Only the advertising segment shows a structure that could support a moat, and it is a small part of the group [S2][S6].

Regulation is a two-sided influence. Bank Indonesia's payment-system rules and the QRIS standard have expanded the market and simultaneously commoditised the distribution layer [S6]. Consumer-protection and data rules raise compliance costs for a group handling merchant and member data. On the positive side, the electric-vehicle build-out is supported by policy incentives, and the group's swap-station network positions it for a fleet market that does not yet exist at scale [S5].

External influences matter more than for a typical platform. The rupiah has been weak, and MCAS carries dollar-denominated convertible notes and payables; FY2025 other expenses included a large net foreign-exchange loss, and the first nine months of FY2026 included another [S2][S3]. Domestic interest rates at the current level raise the cost of the refinancing the group will need if the notes are not extended [S3]. Neither factor is within management's control, and both hit the parent's equity disproportionately because the operating subsidiaries generate most of the cash.

QRIS was introduced as a single national QR standard so that any Indonesian payment app could be accepted by any merchant. It lowered the cost of accepting digital payments for micro-merchants and shifted the competitive frontier from distribution reach to merchant relationships, data and credit. Aggregators that had built value on physical distribution found their spread compressed, and several pivoted toward advertising, software or lending. Digital out-of-home advertising in Indonesia remains fragmented, with traditional billboard operators, media agencies and a handful of digital networks competing for sites.

The revenue history is a story of contraction. Revenue was IDR12,314.9bn in FY2022 [S4], IDR11,697.1bn in FY2023, IDR7,143.6bn in FY2024 and IDR4,737.7bn in FY2025 [S2], with a further fall to IDR2,132.2bn in the first nine months of FY2026 [S3]. Gross profit has been far more stable than revenue: IDR180.9bn in FY2024, IDR183.9bn in FY2025 and IDR112.6bn in the first nine months of FY2026 [S2][S3]. That divergence is the single most important fact about this company. The revenue that is disappearing carried almost no margin, so the gross-profit base has held up much better than the top line suggests, and the blended margin has risen from 2.5% to 3.9% [S2].

Operating expenses have not fallen as fast. FY2025 operating expenses were IDR171.5bn, and the first nine months of FY2026 imply a higher share of revenue because the cost base is partly fixed [S2][S3]. The result was an operating profit of IDR12.5bn in FY2025 and an operating loss of IDR-9.1bn in the first nine months of FY2026 [S2][S3]. Below the operating line, finance costs of IDR15.5bn and other non-operating charges of IDR-46.8bn turned that into a net loss of IDR-58.8bn, of which IDR-38.4bn was attributable to the parent [S2].

One data correction is required. The data pack's depreciation and amortisation line does not reconcile to the audited notes: property and equipment depreciation alone was IDR81.0bn in FY2025 and IDR86.9bn in FY2024, before intangible amortisation and right-of-use depreciation, which the notes disclose separately [S2]. Because the group reports cash flow on the direct method, the statements carry no single combined D&A total that could be quoted verbatim as one figure, so we key the depreciation line to the property and equipment charge — the largest component — and let the forecast carry the full burden through the depreciation ratio rather than through the historical line. That ratio, 2.4% of revenue in FY2026E, is above the ratio the audited total charge implies on FY2025 revenue, so the forecast is not leaning on an understated history. The pack's reported operating profit was also inconsistent with the audited income statement; we restate operating profit to the filing's figure [S2]. These corrections matter for the starting point of the forecast and for any EV/EBITDA cross-check, though they do not change the direction of the call.

Our forecast assumes the aggregator continues to shrink but at a decelerating rate, and that cloud advertising and SaaS grow as the screen network and merchant base are monetised. Revenue growth is -42.3% in FY2026E, -5.0% in FY2027E and then positive from FY2028E, reaching IDR2,949.1bn by FY2030E. The blended gross margin rises from 5.4% to 8.0% as the mix shifts, and operating expenses fall from 5.9% of revenue to 5.0% as the fixed base is spread over a stabilised top line. On those assumptions operating profit turns positive in FY2027E and reaches IDR88.5bn by FY2030E, an operating margin of 3.0% [S2][S3].

Cash flow is the weak point. Operating cash flow was IDR-38.0bn in FY2024 and IDR21.3bn in FY2025, and capital expenditure was IDR43.3bn [S2]. Inventories were IDR461.2bn at 30 September 2026, up from the FY2025 balance while revenue was falling [S2][S3]. Inventory rising while revenue falls is a classic divergence flag: either the group is holding stock it cannot sell, or it is financing its distribution partners. Our forecast holds net working capital at the last actual share of revenue, 24.0%, in every forecast year and in the terminal year; no release is assumed in the base case or in either scenario. On that basis free cash flow is thin in FY2026E and turns positive only as the margin recovery reaches the operating line.

The balance sheet is where the risk concentrates. At 30 September 2026 cash was IDR143.5bn, total liabilities IDR948.0bn and equity attributable to owners IDR144.5bn, with non-controlling interests of IDR868.1bn [S3]. Convertible notes of IDR240.9bn are classified as current, and the notes to the accounts describe a series of extensions: the largest holder agreed to extend to 31 July 2026, and on 30 September 2026 the issuer submitted a further extension request that had not been resolved at the reporting date [S3]. Against that, the parent's equity is thin and the group's ability to repay in cash is limited. On the FY2025 accounts net debt was IDR153.3bn and net debt to EBITDA 1.6x on restated EBITDA [S2]; at 30 September 2026 net debt is materially higher — the group's interest-bearing debt less the IDR143.5bn of cash — and that higher figure is the one carried into the valuation bridge, reflecting the convertible notes and the September investment build [S3].

Capital allocation has been defensive. No dividend was declared at the 2025 annual general meeting, and none is assumed [S2]. The group bought back a small number of shares in FY2025 [S2]. Capital expenditure has been modest relative to depreciation, which flatters free cash flow but raises a question about the maintenance of the screen and swap-station estate. The parent's economic interest in the listed subsidiaries did not change in FY2025 — the reductions in the NFC and Telefast stakes date from earlier transactions — so the recent pattern is one of holding the assets and managing liquidity, not of realising them [S2].

Earnings quality, on the house method card. The accruals ratio is not a concern: the FY2025 net loss of IDR-58.8bn against operating cash flow of IDR21.3bn means earnings are more conservative than cash, not less. The divergence flags are working capital (inventory growing while revenue falls), related-party intensity (trade payables to related parties of IDR184.0bn against total liabilities of IDR749.0bn, and related-party receivables of IDR98.7bn) and the reliance on convertible notes from offshore funds [S2][S3]. The auditor is KAP Mirawati Sensi Idris, a Moore member firm; we found no modified opinion in the annual report we reviewed [S2]. We found no evidence of fabricated cash or fictitious revenue, so the flags are optics and structure class rather than manipulation class. They still justify a discount.

We value MCAS on a consolidated discounted cash flow at a weight of 65.0% and price-to-book (P/BV) on equity attributable to owners at 35.0%. The industry template prescribes a DCF and an EV/sales cross-check; we have replaced the EV/sales weight and explain why below. This is a deliberate override, recorded in the assumptions file, not a modelling convenience.

The cost of capital is high because the capital structure is distorted. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2% and the country risk premium 2.5%; the house cost-of-capital model applies a 1.6% default spread subtracted from the risk-free rate, so the cost of equity is 7.4% less 1.6% plus a levered beta of 3.07 times the sum of the two premia, which is 26.4%. Those are house inputs applied to the data pack's price and the macro deck's series, not company disclosures, and the spread is the house convention rather than a company-specific adjustment [S0]. The beta is levered off a debt-to-market-capitalisation ratio of 2.00, the engine's ceiling, because group debt now exceeds the parent's market capitalisation; debt is 66.7% of the structure and the weighted average cost of capital is 13.7% [S0].

Two cost-of-debt figures appear in this note and they answer different questions. The 9.4% pre-tax rate inside the WACC is the marginal rate a refinancing would carry today, set above the coupon because the notes are current and the extension unresolved [S3]. The forecast interest line uses 6.0%, which is what the group actually paid on its opening debt in FY2025 and annualised in the first nine months of FY2026 [S2][S3]. The first is a discount-rate input, the second a P&L assumption; we do not force them to one number, and the gap is itself part of the risk case.

The house card pins the rupiah cost of capital to a band and asks that an out-of-band rate be argued. Our WACC of 13.7% sits above the top of that band, and the cost of equity of 26.4% is further outside it. We keep it there deliberately: with debt at two-thirds of the structure, any attempt to force the WACC inside the band would require a beta or a country premium the inputs do not support, on a company whose convertible notes are current and whose extension request was unresolved at the reporting date [S3]. We state the direction of the choice plainly: a lower discount rate raises the value here.

The DCF produces a consolidated enterprise value of IDR647.8bn, of which the terminal value is 44.4%. The debt base is the LK's own: total interest-bearing liabilities of IDR422.4bn less cash of IDR143.5bn and restricted time deposits of IDR5.0bn is the Pinjaman bersih the leverage note reports [S3]. After that net debt and the minority claim, parent equity value is Rp224 per share. The minority claim deducted is not the book balance of IDR868.1bn, which exceeds the enterprise value it is a claim on. It is the ownership chain's share of the operating equity value: the group holds 51.6% of NFC directly and 29.3% of DMM only through NFC, so its effective interest in the advertising segment is the product of the two, while the other operations sit inside NFC where the minority holds the remainder. Weighted by nine-month segment gross profit that is close to two-thirds, and the LK itself allocates IDR34.4bn of the IDR53.8bn nine-month net loss to non-controlling interests [S3]. We apply that share to the operating equity value — the enterprise value less the LK net debt — and deduct the result; the assumptions file sets out the arithmetic line by line.

The investment portfolio is carried at the ownership of the entity that holds each stake, which is the correction this version makes. The parent-direct associates and listed shares are wholly ours. ZKDigimax Pte Ltd, the largest single item inside the subsidiary-held associate sleeve, is 20.0% owned by DMM per the annual report [S2], and DMM reaches the group at 29.3% of NFC's 51.6% holding, so that stake returns at the product of the two rather than at the parent's share of the whole group. The remaining subsidiary-held associates and shares sit in subsidiaries whose holder the LK does not name, so they are carried at the blend the LK itself implies when it allocates IDR34.4bn of the IDR53.8bn consolidated loss to non-controlling interests [S3]; the convertible bonds are held in DMM and return at the same effective interest. The endpoints of that judgement are visible: if every subsidiary-held stake were held directly by NFC it would return at 51.6%, and if every one were held through DMM it would return at the product of 51.6% and 29.3%. Counting the portfolio gross while netting the minority claim was an error; so was deducting the book minority against an enterprise value the portfolio helps create. This version does neither.

Why these weights. The DCF is the only method that carries the ownership chain and the minority claim, which is where most of this valuation's uncertainty sits, so it takes the majority weight. P/BV is a floor check, not a co-primary: parent book value is the residual claim after IDR868.1bn of non-controlling interests, it is depressed by cumulative losses, and it carries the stakes at book rather than at value, so weighting it equally to the cash-flow method would let an accounting residual set half the target. We say plainly what the house standard asks for and what we cannot give it: a third cross-check is not available here. EV/sales on pass-through distribution is a category error; P/E has no denominator because parent earnings are negative; and EV/EBITDA, on an EBITDA that is barely positive, would be dominated by the bridge rather than by the business. One primary and one cross-check is the honest set, and the divergence between them, -58.7%, is what the rest of this section and the scenario section are about.

What today's price implies. The price sits between the two methods: the DCF value at our forecast margin path is Rp224 and the P/BV floor is Rp92, and after the twelve-month roll-forward the blended value is Rp178. At Rp199 the market is capitalising the operating business below the value we calculate once the LK net debt and the ownership-chain minority are deducted, and crediting the investment portfolio at less than the parent share we compute. For the price to be right on the DCF alone, the blended gross margin would have to stay at the FY2026E level of 5.4% rather than reaching 8.0%. That is a margin-path call, and it is the one we are underwriting.

Two tests on the DCF. The multiple-survival test, stated on an undiscounted basis so that the entry and exit multiples sit on the same footing: the terminal value is 44.4% of the IDR647.8bn enterprise value in present-value terms, and grossed up at the 13.7% WACC to the terminal year it implies an exit multiple on FY2035E EBITDA of IDR179.4bn that is a small fraction of the 23.6x the market pays for FY2026E EBITDA today. We are assuming a de-rating, not multiple expansion, so the terminal value is not doing the work a bull would want it to do. The reinvestment test: capex is 1.2% of revenue, below the depreciation charge, so the forecast does not buy growth with assets; it buys it with working capital, which the model holds at the last actual share of revenue in every year. Excess returns fade with the margin: terminal growth of 4.0% is below long-run nominal rupiah GDP, and the terminal EBITDA margin of 5.0% is the forecast's own plateau rather than a peak year.

Price-to-book (P/BV) is the cross-check. The method applies a peer median multiple of 0.55 to equity attributable to owners of IDR144.5bn, giving Rp92 per share. The peer set is five Indonesian listed digital platforms and deliberately excludes MCAS's own listed holdings. NFCX and Telefast are the assets MCAS already owns: NFCX trades at a large premium to its own book on the same market that prices MCAS, and we rate it SELL, so including it in the median would import the valuation we are arguing against into the multiple applied to the parent [S0]. The exclusion lowers the median materially and is the honest comparison — what the market pays for a standalone Indonesian digital platform, not for a holding company that contains one. Parent book value is itself depressed by cumulative losses and carries the stakes at book rather than at value, which is why this method sets the floor while the DCF sets the target and carries the larger weight.

The cross-checks explain the divergence, which is -58.7% between the two methods. Price-to-book anchors the downside: it is roughly what a holder would receive if the parent did nothing but liquidate its book equity, and it is the reason we do not carry a target near the DCF alone. The DCF carries what book cannot: the operating businesses at their cash-flow value and the investment portfolio. An EV/EBITDA cross-check would be available in principle, but MCAS's EBITDA is small and volatile and the multiple would be applied to a denominator that is barely positive, so the resulting equity value is dominated by the bridge rather than by the business. An EV/sales approach, the template's prescribed cross-check, values MCAS at a peer multiple of a revenue line that is mostly pass-through distribution sold at a blended gross margin of 5.4% — for a distributor that is a category error, not a cross-check, and we dropped it rather than let it drive the target.

The sensitivity grid now moves, which is itself the test that the valuation is live rather than floored. It shows the DCF value per share against the discount rate and terminal growth, and the twelve-month value against revenue growth and gross margin. The two inputs carrying most of the value are the terminal gross margin and the discount rate; both are argued above, and neither is a heroic assumption relative to what the group has already achieved — the 9M2026 blended gross margin is above the FY2025 level that the forecast starts from [S2][S3].

What the current price implies. At Rp199 the market capitalises MCAS at IDR172.5bn, which is 1.20 times our FY2026E book value attributable to owners. On the engine's enterprise-value definition — market capitalisation plus net debt plus book non-controlling interests, crediting nothing for the investment portfolio — the market pays 23.6x FY2026E EBITDA of IDR51.9bn, while our DCF carries an operating enterprise value of IDR647.8bn [S0]. The gap is the depressed EBITDA base, not a hidden asset. Set against the scenario values, the price is closer to the base case at Rp225 than to either the floor or the bull case; the market is not paying for a platform recovery, and with the debt base corrected it is not giving the shares away either. That is the HOLD.

Indonesian small and mid-cap technology names often trade on revenue or on sum-of-the-parts logic because earnings are thin or negative. That works when the parts are separable and liquid. It works less well when the value sits inside consolidated subsidiaries with large minority shareholders, because the parent's economic interest is diluted and the market cannot easily arbitrage the difference. Holding-company discounts of several tens of percent are common in Indonesia for exactly this reason, and they widen when the parent has liquidity needs of its own.

The downside risks, in order of importance to the call. Liquidity and refinancing: the convertible notes of IDR240.9bn are current and exceed cash of IDR143.5bn, and an extension request was outstanding at the reporting date [S3]; a failure to extend would force a discounted repayment, a dilutive conversion or an asset sale, any of which is bad for the parent's equity. Likelihood: high that a further extension is negotiated, moderate that the terms deteriorate. Impact: high.

Operational: the aggregator could shrink faster than we assume if merchants continue to migrate to bank and e-wallet rails, and the advertising network could under-fill if advertiser demand weakens with the macro cycle. Likelihood: moderate. Impact: medium, because the aggregator carries little gross profit, but the advertising segment is now the profit engine.

Regulatory and competitive: Bank Indonesia's payment rules and the QRIS standard have been growth-positive for the market and margin-negative for distributors [S6]; further interoperability or pricing rules could compress the remaining spread. Likelihood: moderate. Impact: medium.

Currency and rates: dollar-denominated notes and payables expose the group to rupiah weakness, and the FY2025 and 9M2026 accounts show material foreign-exchange losses [S2][S3]. Likelihood: high that some loss recurs. Impact: medium, because the amounts are large relative to parent equity.

Governance and related parties: related-party trade payables of IDR184.0bn and receivables of IDR98.7bn are large relative to the parent's equity [S2]. Related-party terms that favour the controlling group would transfer value away from minorities. Likelihood: low to moderate. Impact: high if it occurs, because the parent's equity cushion is thin.

Our scenarios are mirrored on the same three drivers. In the bear case, with probability 30.0%, revenue growth is four percentage points lower in every forecast year, gross margin a percentage point lower and operating expenses half a point of revenue higher, and the notes are not extended on acceptable terms. In the bull case, with probability 20.0%, the same three drivers move the other way by the same amounts, cloud advertising and SaaS scale faster as QRIS-led merchant digitisation lifts demand, and the notes convert cleanly. The base case carries the remaining probability at 50.0%. Net working capital is held at the same share of revenue in all three cases, so no scenario carries a release.

The bear is a floor, and we say so rather than dress it as a forecast. Under those shocks the DCF's equity value goes to zero, because the debt and minority claims exceed the present value of the cash flows; the only positive method left is P/BV at Rp92, and the bear of Rp41 is that value at its 35.0% weight in the blend. The bear is therefore a statement about the floor rather than about the most likely downside: a holder who believed book value would be realised would put the downside nearer the book value itself. What the scenario does show is that the equity has no cushion in the operating business, and that the notes and the related-party exposure would bite hardest there. The base case is Rp225 and the bull case Rp559, and at Rp199 the market is closer to our base case than to the floor.

Signposts that would change the view. We would revisit the rating downward on a going-concern or emphasis-of-matter paragraph in the FY2026 audit, on a note repayment funded by selling the listed stakes into a weak market, on a related-party transaction that moves cash out of the parent, or on evidence that the investment balance is not realisable in cash. We would revisit it upward on a decision to monetise or distribute the stake in the listed subsidiaries, on two consecutive quarters of double-digit cloud-advertising growth with stable margins, or on NFC's own fundamentals converging on its market price, which is the point at which a sum-of-the-parts case would become our primary method rather than a cross-check.

Ownership and control are concentrated through a listed investment vehicle. PT Quantum Clovera Investama Tbk is disclosed as the controlling shareholder with 8.3% of the shares, and members of the board hold small additional stakes [S2]. The free float is 32.1% and three-month average daily traded value is IDR0.8bn [S0], which is thin for an institutional position and is the reason the valuation carries a liquidity discount. We note that the data pack's insider percentage is inconsistent with the annual report's shareholder table; we use the filing.

Related-party dealings are material. Trade payables to related parties were IDR184.0bn at the end of FY2025, equal to a substantial share of total liabilities of IDR749.0bn, and amounts due from related parties were IDR98.7bn [S2]. The convertible notes are held by offshore investment funds, several of which have extended maturity dates [S3]. These are disclosed and audited, but they mean that a large part of the group's financing and working capital runs through related or affiliated parties, which raises the cost of capital and the governance discount.

Audit and reporting. The FY2025 consolidated financial statements were audited by KAP Mirawati Sensi Idris with Novita as the signing partner [S2]. We found no modified opinion or restatement in the annual report we reviewed. The interim accounts are unaudited, as usual on the Indonesia Stock Exchange, and the first nine months of FY2026 have not been reviewed by us beyond the disclosed figures [S3]. The group has not paid a dividend since at least the last annual meeting, and none is assumed in our forecast [S2].

Board and alignment. The board includes directors with small shareholdings and the controlling shareholder is represented through its stake [S2]. We did not find disclosed share pledges by the controlling shareholder in the annual report we reviewed, but the controlling entity is itself listed and its own leverage is outside our coverage. Alignment is weakened by the parent's thin equity: management's incentives are more closely tied to the operating subsidiaries, where the minorities sit, than to the parent's per-share value.

ESG exposures are modest in absolute terms but specific to the business. The group's direct emissions are small and its disclosed energy intensity is low [S2]. The material exposures are electronic waste from screens and devices, labour practices in the distribution network, data privacy for merchant and member data, and the governance of the electric-vehicle partnership [S5]. The electric-vehicle segment is presented as a sustainability positive, and it is, but it is also capital-consuming and depends on policy support that may change.

Indonesian listed companies with a controlling shareholder often carry a governance discount because minority investors cannot easily influence decisions on related-party transactions, rights issues or subsidiary listings. The discount widens when the parent's equity is thin and when the group's financing runs through affiliated parties, because the parent has less room to absorb a value transfer. Auditors in Indonesia are licensed by the finance ministry and supervised by the capital-market regulator; a change of auditor tier is a signal worth monitoring.

The dated catalysts are the FY2026 audited results, expected by the end of the first quarter of 2027, the convertible note decision, which we expect before the end of 2026, and the 2027 annual general meeting. Each is a test of a specific part of the thesis. The results will show whether the aggregator decline is decelerating and whether cloud advertising is filling the gap; the note decision will show whether the liquidity overhang is removed or merely pushed out; the meeting will show whether the controlling group is willing to support the parent's equity or to extract from it [S2][S3].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are: aggregator revenue and gross profit, to see whether the mix shift is real or merely a smaller version of the same business; cloud advertising revenue, screen count and fill, which are the only genuinely high-margin assets in the group; SaaS revenue and notification volume, as a proxy for the software franchise; inventory days and operating cash flow, because a genuine inventory unwind is the largest single source of upside we have not put in the base case; net debt and the convertible note balance, as the binding constraint on the equity; the investment balance disclosed each quarter, since it is now the largest single item behind the DCF value; and any related-party balances, as the governance tell [S2][S3].

We will also track the listed subsidiaries. NFC Indonesia's own results and share price matter twice over: they drive the consolidated numbers and they are the reference point the market uses for the parent's asset value. We rate NFC SELL on its own cash flows, so we do not carry its market price into this target; if NFC's fundamentals improve and its valuation becomes supported by cash flow rather than liquidity, the sum-of-the-parts case becomes the right primary method and the target would rise further [S2][S3].

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for MCAS.JK

bear.narrative: Aggregator revenue keeps falling at a double-digit pace as partners insource, cloud-advertising fill rates stall, and the convertible notes are not extended, forcing a discounted asset sale. Margin recovery stops near 5%.

bull.narrative: Cloud advertising and SaaS scale faster as QRIS-led merchant digitisation lifts demand, the aggregator stabilises, and the convertible notes convert at a premium, removing the liquidity overhang. Blended gross margin reaches double digits.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 revenue of Rp2,132.2bn is 40.6% below 9M2025 as the low-margin digital product aggregator shrinks; Q4 run-rate implies FY2026E near Rp2.7tn. Aggregator decline moderates in FY2027E before cloud advertising and SaaS growth turns the group positive from FY2028E.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Margin has risen from 2.53% FY2024 to 3.88% FY2025 to 5.28% in 9M2026 because cloud advertising earns a 39.1% gross margin and SaaS 17.7% while the aggregator earns 0.76%; continued mix shift lifts the blended margin toward 8% by FY2030E.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating expenses were Rp121.7bn in 9M2026, 5.71% of revenue, as the cost base stayed sticky while revenue fell; cost actions hold the absolute base near Rp150bn while advertising and SaaS revenue scale, so the ratio falls to 5.0% by FY2030E.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 depreciation of property and equipment was Rp81.0bn, plus Rp5.8bn intangible amortisation and Rp1.7bn right-of-use depreciation; on a falling revenue base the ratio is about 2.4% and drifts down with capex discipline.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capital expenditure was Rp43.3bn or 0.91% of revenue, and FY2024 Rp29.5bn; a modest 1.0-1.2% of revenue funds digital signage, EV charging and IT while the group preserves cash.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Net working capital (current assets less current liabilities, excluding cash and short-term debt) was Rp685.6bn at 30 September 2026 against annualised 9M2026 revenue of about Rp2.8tn, i.e. 24% of revenue, and the FY2025 balance sheet shows the same 24%. Inventories of Rp461.2bn rose 33% while revenue fell, so working capital absorbed rather than released cash. We hold the ratio at the last actual 24% through the forecast: a cash release would have to come from an inventory unwind we cannot source, and the 9M2026 balance sheet shows inventories still rising [S3][S2].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Statutory Indonesian corporate income tax is 22%; the LK effective rate of about 12% in 9M2026 reflects deferred-tax and non-deductible losses, so forecasts use the statutory rate once the group returns to profit.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance expenses of Rp15.5bn on opening debt of Rp352.8bn equal 4.4%, rising to 4.7% annualised in 9M2026; bank and convertible funding is priced at mid-single digits in rupiah.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income of Rp6.7bn on opening cash of Rp207.0bn equals 3.2%, while 9M2026 interest income of Rp2.1bn on a smaller average balance is lower; 2.5% reflects current rupiah deposit rates.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new debt assumed; the Rp240.9bn of convertible notes is expected to be extended or converted rather than refinanced with new borrowings.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Net other expenses were Rp46.8bn in FY2025 and Rp14.8bn in FY2024, driven by rupiah depreciation on dollar payables and convertible notes; 9M2026 net foreign-exchange loss was Rp21.8bn plus Rp6.1bn of associate and provisioning losses, so a normalised Rp25-28bn annual charge is carried.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Rebuilt from the ownership chain, not carried at 45%: DMM, the cloud-advertising segment that earned Rp50.0bn of the Rp112.6bn 9M2026 gross profit, is 29.30% owned by NFC, which MCAS holds at 51.62%, so the group owns 15.13% and minorities 84.87%; the other segments sit inside NFC where the minority is 48.38%. Weighting those shares by 9M2026 segment gross profit gives 64.6%, and the LK itself allocates 64.0% of the 9M2026 net loss to non-controlling interests (Rp34.4bn of Rp53.8bn), so 64% is used flat across the forecast [S3].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The 18 June 2025 AGMS declared no dividend for FY2024 and the group has posted net losses since; no payout is assumed through FY2030E while balance sheet repair takes priority.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue or buyback assumed; shares outstanding are 867.0m and the convertible notes are carried as liabilities at 30 September 2026.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for Indonesian rupiah cash flows, consistent with long-run nominal GDP growth and below the forecast-period growth rate.

challenges.challenge: Half the valuation (dcf_fcff weight 0.5) is floored at Rp0 by deducting book NCI of Rp897.8bn from an EV of Rp774.1bn, while the same model applies only 45% of net profit to minorities (minority_pct 0.45). On the model's own minority share the parent's claim is 774.1 x 0.55 - 270.3 + 175.7 = Rp331.1bn, or Rp382 per share, which would flip the rating. The assumptions file itself says the Rp868.1bn book NCI is 'inflated by past equity transactions with minorities' and then deducts it anyway.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt the bridge. The DCF now deducts the minorities at the share of equity value the LK actually allocates to non-controlling interests rather than at the book NCI: a bridge item of +Rp684.7bn replaces the Rp868.1bn book deduction, computed as 868.1 less 45% of [EV 647.8 less net debt 240.3]. Parent equity value is now positive: Rp448.6bn, or Rp517 per share, against Rp0 floored before. Section 4 publishes that value and explains why a minority claim larger than the enterprise value it is a claim on cannot be the right deduction, and the investment summary says the prior SELL was the floor, not the business [S3][S2].

challenges.challenge: The two listed stakes the report promises to 'take seriously' are never valued anywhere. 51.62% of NFCX is worth Rp615.5bn at the pack price (Rp1,800 x 662.4m shares) and 42.19% of TFAS Rp30.9bn at the house target of Rp44 - together about 4x MCAS's Rp172.5bn market cap. The P/B method applies 0.775x to consolidated parent book and the DCF consolidates NFCX's cash flows, so no observable value of these assets enters the target; section 4's reason ('trades at a valuation its own cash flows do not support') carries no number.
challenges.answer: We deliberately did not build a market-mark SOTP, and the reason is sourced. NFC carries 86% of group revenue and we cover it SELL: its market equity is about 4.5x book and 213x FY2025 earnings, and its own house DCF gives an enterprise value of Rp176.7bn against a market enterprise value near Rp1,394bn. Marking MCAS 51.62% stake at that price would import into the parent target the valuation our own coverage rejects, the same circularity that contaminated the peer median in C10. At house marks the stakes are worth Rp135.5bn (NFC at book) plus about Rp31bn (TFAS at our Rp44 target); the consolidated DCF already owns those cash flows and apportions them at the economic minority share, and the investment portfolio enters at its 30 September 2026 book of Rp224.4bn [S2][S3].

challenges.challenge: FY2027E FCFF of Rp125.5bn against EBITDA of Rp75.3bn is driven by a ~Rp135bn working-capital release (nwc_pct 24% to 20%) - the same inventory (Rp461.2bn, up 33% while revenue fell) that section 3 calls a divergence flag and possibly unsellable stock. The PV of FY2027E alone is Rp115.3bn, 25% of the DCF's Rp468.2bn PV sum, so the release is load-bearing for the EV that the minority deduction then wipes out.
challenges.answer: nwc_pct is now held at the last actual 24% of revenue in every forecast year and in the terminal year; the 135bn release is gone. Consolidated enterprise value falls from Rp774.1bn to Rp647.8bn and the FY2027E free cash flow the reviewer identified as load-bearing no longer exists. Section 3 states that no release is assumed, that inventories rose again in 9M2026, and that an unwind is the largest single source of upside we have deliberately left in the bull case [S3].

challenges.challenge: Every bridge input is the 30 June 2026 data-pack balance sheet (market.bs_date 2026-06-30: cash 113.47, debt 383.76, NCI 897.84, equity 148.78), while the report's own text and the 9M26 facts use 30 September 2026 (cash 143.5, NCI 868.1, parent equity 144.5). The post_bs_review says the interim accounts were read and no bridge item is material, but restated_bs is empty. The stated arithmetic is therefore wrong: 144.5 x 0.7754 / 866.9952 = Rp129.2, not Rp133, and the target would be about Rp100.6.
challenges.answer: The 30 September 2026 balance sheet is now keyed as facts (bs_cash 143.5, bs_equity 144.5, bs_minority_bs 868.1) so the engine rebuilds the bridge from the latest LK instead of the 30 June pack, and the Rp48.7bn increase in investments is carried as a bridge item. The P/B arithmetic is now 0.554 x parent book of Rp144.5bn, giving Rp92 per share, and the report text matches the model rather than the superseded June figures [S3].

challenges.challenge: D&A is keyed at Rp81.04bn, which is the property-and-equipment depreciation total from the PP&E note (Jumlah 81.035.749.973 / 86.895.554.340), but the da_pct basis in the same assumptions file says total D&A is 81.0 + 5.8 intangible amortisation + 1.7 right-of-use = Rp88.5bn. FCFF (ebit x (1-t) + da - capex - delta_nwc) is thus understated by ~Rp7.5bn a year and FY2025 EBITDA of Rp93.5bn by 8%. Section 3's claim that 'the pack reports D&A of IDR81.0bn, which is a fraction of the charge in the audited accounts' also contradicts the restatement table, where the pack figure was 28.66.
challenges.answer: Implemented in part, and the part that carries value is fixed. The direct-method cash flow statements carry no single combined D&A total, so keying 88.5 would mean fabricating a verbatim quote; we keep the property and equipment depreciation fact (Rp81.0bn / Rp86.9bn) and correct the section 3 paragraph so it no longer claims the pack figure is a fraction of the charge, which contradicted the restatement table. Forecast free cash flow does not depend on that history: it uses da_pct of revenue, 2.4% in FY2026E, above the 1.87% the audited total charge implies on FY2025 revenue, so FCFF is not understated [S2].

challenges.challenge: WACC 13.7% and COE 26.4% sit outside the method card's IDR 11-13% band and the COE is roughly double every covered peer (BELI 13.2%, BUKA 12.2%, EMTK 13.9%, GOTO 15.9%). The COE is 7.45% - 1.62% + 3.072 x (4.23% + 2.46%), where beta 3.072 comes from a D/E of 2.00 that is capped debt over market cap (383.8/172.5 = 2.22), not the 'book debt against shrunken book equity' the report describes. That COE then rolls the blended value from 66.5 to 84.1; at a band-compliant 12.5% the target is about Rp92. Separately, kd is 9.45% (rf + house spread) in the model while the driver table says 6.0% (actual 4.4-4.7%); at 6.0% the WACC is about 11.9%, inside the band.
challenges.answer: The WACC of 13.7% sits at the top of the card band and the COE above it, and that is the argued choice. Debt is 66.7% of the structure at a capped D/E of 2.00; an in-band COE of 13% would put the WACC near 9.2%, below the band, on a name whose convertible notes are current with an unresolved extension request. Between two out-of-band outcomes we discount more, and the error direction is conservative. kd of 9.45% is rf 7.45% plus the house corporate spread of 2.0%; the 6.0% driver is the LK actual finance cost (Rp15.5bn on Rp352.8bn opening debt, 4.4%), used for the P&L interest line, not for the cost of capital. The discount-rate sensitivity is the WACC / terminal-growth grid in section 4 [S2][S3].

challenges.challenge: The bear scenario produces exactly the base value (v0 66.53 and tp 84.08 in both) because the DCF is floored at zero, so the 30% bear weight has no effect while a 20% bull adds Rp47.4bn of the Rp114.7bn weighted value. The probability weighting therefore lifts the target 23% above the analyst's own most-likely base, and the report never states that the base case is Rp84, -58%. Claims elsewhere ('the sensitivity table is flat', 'the reverse-DCF cannot bracket the current price') are contradicted by the engine's own grid (GM +2pp and revenue +4pp gives Rp348.7) and by the bull case's positive DCF.
challenges.answer: The scenarios now differ because nothing is floored: bear v0 180.5 and tp 228.2, base 304.8 and 385.3, bull 508.7 and 642.9, weighted at 0.3 / 0.5 / 0.2. Section 5 states both the base-case value and the probability weighting, and section 4 replaces the cannot-bracket language with what the price implies: at Rp199 the market sits at our bear case, which is the honest reading of the evidence [S0][S3].

challenges.challenge: The variant view that the market is 'capitalising the wrong line' and valuing MCAS 'as a platform' is contradicted by the price: at Rp199 the whole company is capitalised at Rp172.5bn, 76% below the Rp714bn market value of its two listed stakes, so the market is already applying a holdco discount. Missing: that the departing aggregator earns 0.76% gross margin (Rp27.6bn of Rp183.9bn group gross profit), so the revenue collapse costs almost no cash; that cloud advertising already earns 39.1% margin and SaaS 17.7%; that a note conversion above book would add to book value per share rather than dilute it; and any value for 28,996 screens, 422 swap stations or the Volta fleet.
challenges.answer: The investment summary is rewritten. It quantifies the stakes, states the holdco-discount logic (the market pays less than the sum of the parts, and we explain why the marks we would use are house marks, not the siblings prices), and replaces the platform-multiple claim with what the 9M2026 segment note shows: aggregator and advertising gross margins improved even as their revenue fell. Section 4 states what would have to be true for the price to be right, namely no margin recovery, no inventory unwind and no credit for the portfolio [S3][S2].

challenges.challenge: The bear case names a liquidity event it does not model. The Rp240.9bn of USD notes are current, every holder consented to extend only to 31 July 2026, and the 30 September 2026 extension request was 'still in process' at the financial-statement date, yet the model has net_borrowing 0 and share_change 0 in all scenarios and no FX sensitivity. A 10% rupiah move adds about Rp24bn to the USD notes, roughly 17% of parent equity, against the macro deck's FY2027E usd_idr of 18,350 versus spot 17,633.
challenges.answer: The refinancing branch is described and sized in section 5 but not modelled as a separate shock, because the scenario set must stay mirrored: the bear already carries revenue growth 4pp lower, gross margin 1pp lower and opex 0.5pp of revenue higher, and a one-sided distress shock would break the mirror the method card requires. The liquidity and FX costs enter through the liquidity discount and through a cost of equity that already reflects a capped D/E of 2.00. Section 3 reconciles the 9M2026 liability build (Rp948.0bn) and inventory (Rp461.2bn) with the note position [S3].

challenges.challenge: The method override is unregistered and the P/B peer set is contaminated. The QC gate still reports weights.changed as justified false - the weight_basis prose is not read by the gate. The 0.775x median is GOTO's multiple taken over seven names that include MCAS's own subsidiary NFCX (4.54x) and affiliate TFAS (1.40x); dropping those two gives a median of 0.554 (WIFI), which would cut the P/B value from Rp133 to Rp95 and the target to about Rp85. The card's output contract (reinvestment rate, ROIIC, fade year, implied exit multiple versus entry) is absent.
challenges.answer: The peer set now excludes MCAS own holdings: the median falls to 0.554 from the five remaining Indonesian digital platforms, and the P/B value falls from Rp133 to Rp92. A qc_justifications entry for weights.changed now states the override and its sources, since the gate does not read weight_basis. The multiple-survival test is in section 4: the terminal value implies an exit multiple of about five times FY2035E EBITDA against 23.6x on today's depressed FY2026E EBITDA, so we assume a de-rating rather than multiple expansion [S0][S2].

challenges.challenge: Ownership and source labelling are wrong in small but checkable ways: 'after sell-downs in FY2025' contradicts S2, which shows TFAS sold down to 42.19% in 2021 and NFCX bought up to 51.62% in 2024, both unchanged through FY2025; 'the largest holder had already extended' understates that every noteholder consented to the 31 July 2026 date; the FY2022 revenue of Rp12,314.9bn is cited to S2, which only carries 2023-25 (it is in S4); and the 26.4% COE, 9.4% kd and 13.7% WACC are cited to S0, which does not contain them.
challenges.answer: Stake history corrected: NFC was bought up to 51.62% in 2024 and TFAS sold down to 42.19% in 2021, both unchanged through FY2025, and the fact labels and section 1 no longer say FY2025 sell-downs; the sentence about FY2025 disposals raising cash is removed. FY2022 revenue is now cited to S4. The cost of capital is labelled as house inputs built on the data pack price and the macro deck rather than as company disclosure, and the note extension is described as the all-holder consent it was [S2][S4].

challenges.challenge: Presentation errors sit in load-bearing sentences: 'market capitalises MCAS at IDR172,532,044,800.0bn' and ADTV 'IDR811,815,922.2bn' should be Rp172.5bn and Rp0.81bn; 'bear case, with probability 0.3%' and 'bull, with probability 0.2%' are 0.30 and 0.20 in the model; '1.30 times equity attributable to owners' is a FY2026E forecast-book ratio (172.5/132.4) whereas the reported ratios are 1.19x at 9M26 and 1.05x for FY2025; and '24.2x forecast EV/EBITDA' is on an EV that adds the Rp897.8bn NCI and deducts investments, so it is 8.5x on market cap plus net debt.
challenges.answer: Units and percentages fixed: market cap and ADTV now use the billion-rupiah format, scenario probabilities render from the model as percentages, the P/B ratio is labelled as FY2026E book value rather than reported equity, and the EV/EBITDA ratio now states its enterprise-value definition (minority interest included, investment balance netted) so a reader can reproduce it from the model [S0].

challenges.challenge: Q2 not fixed: the 36% group economic share applied to Rp166.25bn of subsidiary-held associates and shares is still the 1 minus 64% minority ratio, not the ownership of the holding entity; the report and the bridge label do not name the holder of ZKDigimax (Rp70.84bn of the Rp99.93bn) or show the 51.62%/15.13% endpoints. The choice moves the bridge by Rp25-35bn, or Rp29-40 per share on a 195 target.
challenges.answer: The LK groups the Rp99.93bn associate sleeve under subsidiaries without naming each holder; the FY2025 annual report states DMM owns 20.00% of ZKDigimax, so that Rp70.84bn item now returns at the group 15.13% effective interest in DMM (51.62% x 29.30%), not at 36%. Unnamed residual stakes stay at the blended 36% and section 4 now shows both endpoints, 51.62% direct and 15.13% through DMM. [S2][S3]

challenges.challenge: Q6 not fixed: the P/B cross-check carries 50% weight, equal to the primary DCF, with no reason given for that weight, and the lint still reports only two methods against the house standard of a primary plus two cross-checks. The weight is load-bearing: DCF is Rp241 (+21% vs price) and the 50/50 blend is what produces the -2.2% HOLD. Section 4 also says P/B sets the floor and the DCF sets the target, which is inconsistent with an equal-weight blend.
challenges.answer: Weights are now 65% DCF and 35% P/B, so the primary sets the target and the cross-check sets the floor, which is what section 4 now says. The reason is stated: the DCF is the only method carrying the ownership chain and the minority claim, while parent book is the residual after Rp868.1bn of NCI and is depressed by cumulative losses. Section 4 also states that a third method is unavailable on this balance sheet. [S3]

challenges.challenge: Q5 not fixed: section 5 still says price-to-book does not respond to operating shocks so the bear case falls to Rp58; mechanically the bear is Rp58 because the DCF equity floors at zero and P/B is the only positive method. The report never states that, so the bear is presented as a modelled outcome when it is a floor artefact.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now states the mechanism rather than a narrative: under the bear shocks the DCF equity value floors at zero, and the bear is the P/B value at its 35% weight. It also says the true downside is nearer book value than the mechanical blend, so the floor artefact is disclosed. [S0]

challenges.challenge: Q5 second limb not fixed: sections 1, 4 and 5 still contrast the bear and the price-implied case with a working-capital release, but nwc_pct is 24% in every forecast year and in the terminal year, so no year carries a release and the bull case carries none either. The price-implied discussion is therefore describing a difference that does not exist.
challenges.answer: Deleted the working-capital-release contrast throughout: section 1 no longer frames working capital that way, section 3 states the ratio is held in every forecast year and the terminal year, section 4 drops the release clause from the margin-path sentence, and section 5 states no scenario carries a release. [S3]

challenges.challenge: Q3 not fixed: section 4 still lists rf 7.45%, ERP 4.23%, CRP 2.46% and beta 3.072 and claims a COE of 26.4%, but those inputs give 28.0%; the engine default spread of -1.62% that produces 26.38% is not disclosed, so the headline cost of capital does not reproduce from the stated inputs.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now shows the house -1.62% default spread subtracted from the risk-free rate, so 7.45% less 1.62% plus a levered beta of 3.07 times 6.69% reproduces the 26.4% cost of equity, and it labels the risk-free rate, ERP, CRP, beta and the spread as house inputs rather than company disclosures. [S0]

challenges.challenge: Q1 and Q4 not fixed. The multiple-survival test still compares the PV of the terminal value with an undiscounted entry multiple, overstating the de-rating case (1.6x on the PV basis versus 5.8x undiscounted, against 23.6x entry), without disclosing the basis. Separately, the 9.45% pre-tax cost of debt in the WACC and the 6.0% cost_of_debt that drives the forecast interest line still coexist unreconciled.
challenges.answer: Accepted on both limbs. The multiple-survival test is restated on an undiscounted basis: the terminal value is grossed up at the 13.7% WACC to FY2035E and set against that year EBITDA, with the 23.6x entry multiple on the same undiscounted footing. Section 4 also separates the 9.45% marginal pre-tax cost of debt in the WACC from the 6.0% P&L interest assumption and says why they differ. [S0][S3]

missing_bull_case.note: The bull case is only +1pp gross margin and -0.5pp opex; its narrative ('blended gross margin reaches double digits', notes convert at a premium) is not delivered by those shocks (GM 8% +1pp = 9%). Missing entirely: the observable value of the 51.62% NFCX stake (662.4m shares x Rp1,800 = Rp1,192.3bn mcap, so Rp615.5bn) and 42.19% of TFAS (house TP Rp44, so Rp30.9bn) against MCAS's own Rp172.5bn mcap; that the exiting aggregator earns 0.76% gross margin so its loss costs almost no cash; and any value for the screens, swap stations or Volta fleet beyond capex.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear narrative (notes not extended, discounted asset sale) is not modelled: net_borrowing 0 and share_change 0 in every scenario, so bear value equals base exactly (v0 66.53, tp 84.08 both). Absent: a going-concern or special-notation path; FX on the Rp240.9bn USD notes (a 10% rupiah move is ~17% of parent equity) against the deck's usd_idr FY2027E 18,350; and the 9M26 balance-sheet deterioration (liabilities 948.0 vs 749.0; inventory 461.2 vs 345.7) that the text reports but never connects to liquidity.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E revenue -42.3% implies Q4 2026E of ~Rp601bn, i.e. -47.6% yoy against a 9M trend of -40.6%, with no source for the acceleration. FY2027E FCFF of Rp125.5bn against EBITDA of Rp75.3bn is mostly a ~Rp135bn working-capital release (nwc_pct 24% to 20%), the same inventory the report calls unsellable. D&A is keyed at 81.0 (PP&E only) although the da_pct basis says total D&A is 88.5, and cost of debt is 6.0% in the drivers but 9.4% in the valuation.

evidence_and_citations.note: Load-bearing bridge inputs do not trace to the cited filing: P/B book 148.78, net debt 270.3, NCI 897.8 and cash 113.5 are all the 30 June 2026 data-pack balance sheet (market.bs_date 2026-06-30), while the report and facts use 30 September 2026 (144.5 / 868.1 / 143.5). The stated arithmetic 144.5 x 0.78 = Rp133 is actually Rp129.2. 'Sell-downs in FY2025' is contradicted by the S2 subsidiary table. Free float 32.1% [S0] vs 43.88% public <5% in S2.

valuation_method_fit.note: The minority bridge is internally inconsistent: book NCI 897.8 deducted from EV 774.1 floors the DCF at zero while the same model gives minorities 45% of profit. No SOTP exists for a parent whose value is two listed stakes. The P/B book date is unstated (30 June, not the 9M26 filing). No implied exit multiple, reinvestment rate, ROIIC or fade year (method card items 1-5). The 0.775x peer median includes MCAS's own NFCX (4.54x) and TFAS (1.40x); excluding them the median is 0.554. The weights override is unregistered.

bias_and_tone.note: The target of 103 is 23% above the analyst's own most-likely base of 84, purely because the DCF floor truncates the bear while leaving the bull unbounded; the report never states the base-case value or its -58% return. 'The sensitivity table is flat' is contradicted by the engine grid (GM +2pp and revenue +4pp gives Rp348.7). 'The reverse-DCF cannot bracket the price' is a failed search on revenue growth only. The market is said to value MCAS 'as a platform' when at Rp199 it sits 76% below the market value of its listed stakes.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: COE 26.4% and WACC 13.7% are outside the method card's IDR 11-13% band and roughly double every covered peer (12.2-15.9% COE); the COE is then applied as a 26.4% roll-forward that lifts the base from 66.5 to 84.1. The D/E of 2.00 is a capped debt/market-cap ratio (383.8/172.5 = 2.22), not the 'book debt against shrunken book equity' the text describes. Method weights dcf 0.5 / pbv 0.5 depart from the INTERNET_PLATFORMS config (dcf 0.6 / ev_sales 0.4) with the WARN unjustified. The macro deck's usd_idr path is unused despite USD notes.

conservatism_audit.note: Every stale bridge input runs one way against value: net debt 270.3 when 9M26 cash is Rp30bn higher; NCI 897.8 vs 868.1; book 148.78 vs 144.5; D&A 81.0 PP&E-only so FCFF is understated ~Rp7.5bn a year; and a 22% tax charge is applied even in loss years (FY2026E EBIT -13.7 carries a -3.0 'tax charge'). Unsourced: the 10% liquidity discount and the Q4 2026E revenue step-down. No dilution from Rp240.9bn of convertible notes in any scenario. This stack is what floors the DCF.

calibration.note: The arithmetic gate passes (FY2025A EBITDA margin 1.97% vs model 1.90%, gap -0.07pp) but the calibrated EBITDA is built on PP&E-only D&A, and the extreme_call justification that clears the BLOCK misstates the model's own inputs: it cites parent book of Rp163.7bn and 1.2x, while the engine uses 148.78 and 1.30x; it also says Rp1.09tn book equity, which is FY2025 (9M26 is Rp1.01tn). weights.changed remains justified: false, and post_bs.review is an orphan key.

signoff.notes: Round 2 APPROVED. The three material reasons are resolved in text and model. (1) Ownership arithmetic: ZKDigimax returns at 15.13% (F66 DMM 29.30% x F52 NFC 51.62%) applied to the Rp70.84bn carrying value = Rp10.72bn, QC-recomputed to the filing; the unnamed residual Rp95.41bn returns at the 36% parent share of the LK 64% loss allocation, with both endpoints (15.13% through DMM, 51.62% direct) stated and the Rp39/share range disclosed. The DCF portfolio of Rp69.27bn against the Rp175.7bn in EV is bridged in assumptions, so the portfolio is neither grossed nor double-deducted. (2) Weights agree between model and prose: DCF 65% / P-B 35%, P-B explicitly a floor, and section 4 argues why a third cross-check is unavailable - peers BUKA, GOTO and BELI also run two methods, so the pair is not an outlier. (3) Bear is explained as the floor: the DCF equity goes to zero under the mirrored shocks and the bear Rp41 is P-B at its 35% weight, consistent across S1, S5 and the engine (Rp32.31 x 1.264). Front matter now reads initiation v1 with no published or refresh residue. Peer consistency: HOLD at +6.9% sits between the cash-rich BUY names (BUKA, GOTO, EMTK) and the no-residual SELLs (NFCX, TFAS), and unlike NFCX the parent claim is bridged, so there is no systematic batch tilt. Residual QC FIX items judged non-material to the call: F1 omits the numeric 5.2x implied exit multiple (TV Rp929.0bn / FY2035E EBITDA Rp179.4bn) though it states the de-rating direction - fix at the next scheduled update; F2 30% on the zero-DCF branch is conservative by about Rp14 (target ~Rp227) but rating-invariant, still HOLD, and is now disclosed as a branch probability with the book-value downside (Rp92) stated to the reader. Carry F5 (NOL/tax) and F6 (IDX board/notation sentence, no flag found in S2/S4) to the next update. Never edited report, model, datapack, config or scripts.

bias.note: Both directions checked. Conservative: the 30% bear weight sits on the zero-DCF Rp41 value although S5 itself says the true downside is nearer book (Rp92), worth about Rp14 of target; the residual Rp95.4bn sleeve is carried at 36% against the 51.62% NFC endpoint (+Rp39/share if that endpoint held); FY2026E revenue growth -42.3% vs 9M actual -40.6%; tax 22% vs the LK 9M2026 12.3%. Optimistic offset: the twelve-month roll-forward at the full 26.4% COE adds Rp47/share (house convention) and the base case (Rp225, 50%) sits above price. Net: HOLD at +6.9% is the most likely path; base at 50% with mirrored +/-4pp/1pp/0.5pp shocks means the tree is not degenerate.

findings.finding: Q1 carried in part: S4 now states the multiple-survival test on an undiscounted footing and grosses the terminal value up at the 13.7% WACC, but the resulting exit multiple is no longer given - the prose says 'a small fraction of' 23.6x. TV of Rp929.0bn over FY2035E EBITDA of Rp179.4bn is 5.2x, and the method card's output contract asks for implied exit versus entry multiple explicitly.

S5 says the bear is 'a statement about the floor rather than about the most likely downside' and that a holder believing book would be realised would put the downside nearer book, yet the 30% probability is applied to the Rp41 zero-DCF value. That knowingly understates expected value by about Rp14 of target (Rp227 if the 30% sat on the Rp92 book floor) and leaves the stated view and the weighted target disagreeing.

Q2 is resolved in substance: S3 note 16 p.108 gives ZKDigimax at Rp70.843bn of the Rp99.931bn subsidiary sleeve, S2 p.139 confirms DMM owns 20.00%, and 15.13% x Rp70.84bn = Rp10.72bn reproduces. The residual Rp95.41bn still returns at the 36% loss-allocation ratio rather than an ownership percentage, though both endpoints are now shown.

FY2026E revenue growth of -42.3% is 1.7pp below the 9M2026 actual of -40.6%, and the basis sentence says 'Q4 run-rate implies FY2026E near Rp2.7tn' when 9M revenue of Rp2,132.2bn x 4/3 is Rp2.84tn. Immaterial to the call (about Rp3/share) but the basis is internally inconsistent.

The forecast uses the 22% statutory tax rate while the LK's 9M2026 tax charge of Rp5.87bn on a pre-tax loss of Rp47.93bn is 12.3%, and the group carries Rp27.1bn of deferred tax assets plus cumulative losses. The 22% rate is disclosed and argued but is worth roughly Rp10/share against a 12% effective rate.

Q7 and Q8 carry forward: the rendered report is 6,481 words against the 500-3,500 house range (lint warning) and S6 still does not state the IDX board/notation status (papan pemantauan khusus, notation letters) that the earnings-quality card asks for first.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_sales': 0.4}
flags.justification: DCF 65% / P/B 35%, not an equal split. The DCF is the only method that carries the ownership chain and the minority claim the LK itself allocates at 64% of the 9M2026 loss [S3]; P/B on parent book is a floor check because 86% of consolidated book equity belongs to minorities, so parent book is the residual claim on the group [S3]. EV/sales is invalid on pass-through revenue at a 0.8% margin [S2], P/E has negative parent earnings, and EV/EBITDA on a barely positive EBITDA would be bridge-driven, so the third standard cross-check is not available and we say so in section 4.
